assessment.nobel_worthiness: Precision mapping of the CMB anisotropies turned cosmology into a quantitative science: it fixed the age, geometry and composition of the universe (dark energy, dark matter, baryons) and tested the inflationary initial conditions. The discovery is clear, deeply lasting, and speaks directly to our place in the universe. COBE was already recognized (2006), so this is the logical next step.
assessment.attribution: WMAP leadership (Bennett as PI, Page, Spergel for analysis and parameters) offers a fair three-person configuration. Planck and Jean-Loup Puget's contribution, and the many ground and balloon experiments, complicate credit; the large-collaboration character is a real allocation problem.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed independently by Planck, ACT, SPT and by BAO and supernova data; the interpretation (LCDM) is stable. Recognition is mature, if arguably late.
uncertainties: Whether WMAP alone or WMAP plus Planck should be honoured, and who from Planck.
Persistent tensions (Hubble constant) do not undermine the discovery but show the model is still being tested.
I am relying on my general knowledge of the roles; I have not independently verified them.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The optical lattice clock (magic-wavelength trapping, Katori's proposal and Ye's realization) brought fractional clock uncertainty to the 1e-18 level, with applications from relativistic geodesy to tests of constant variation and dark-matter searches. A clear invention with demonstrated, nature-based tests of fundamental physics.
assessment.attribution: Katori invented the magic-wavelength concept; Ye led the strontium realization and ultra-precise performance. A clean two-person configuration. Hall and Hänsch (2005) covered the comb; ion-clock work (Wineland, 2012) is separate.
assessment.maturity: Many independent clocks worldwide confirm the performance; redefinition of the second is under discussion. Highly mature and timely.
uncertainties: Overlap with ion-clock and comb recognition may be seen as incremental by some.
Whether others (e.g. Pritchard-type neutral-atom contributors or Lemonde/Lisdat groups) deserve a share.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The first horizon-scale images of M87* and Sgr A* give direct empirical evidence on black holes in strong gravity, an observational counterpart to the theoretical work recognized in 2020. As a physicist who works on horizonless mimickers, I find the shadow measurement important and wish to see how tightly it constrains alternatives.
assessment.attribution: Falcke proposed the shadow imaging concept, Doeleman led the EHT VLBI campaign, Moran provided the long-baseline technique foundation. The EHT is a collaboration of hundreds, so a three-person prize is a simplification; credit allocation is unresolved.
assessment.maturity: Two independent targets, repeated multi-epoch M87* images and polarization; however, interpretation precision (spin, model dependence) is still developing. Mostly timely, a bit early for detailed physics.
uncertainties: Collaboration-scale credit; the committee has historically struggled with this.
Model-dependence of mass and spin inference and of alternatives to Kerr.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit QED created strong light-matter coupling on a chip and underlies superconducting quantum processors, dispersive readout and quantum control. A foundational platform with huge impact, partially recognised by the 2025 prize for macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits, which makes the lineage clear but may reduce the available room.
assessment.attribution: Blais, Wallraff, Huang, Girvin and Schoelkopf wrote and demonstrated the 2004 proposal and experiment; Andreas Wallraff is notably absent from the credited list, which weakens the fairness of this configuration as supplied. Among the supplied names, Schoelkopf (experiment) and Blais and Girvin (theory) is plausible.
assessment.maturity: Strongly confirmed in many labs; technology is now commercial. Recognition is timely, though the 2025 prize may weigh against it.
uncertainties: Exclusion of Wallraff from the credited names.
Overlap with the 2025 prize and with the larger quantum-computing story.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Cirac and Zoller proposed the ion-trap quantum gate and the framework for quantum simulation and computation with trapped ions and neutral atoms. Foundational ideas that created experimental programmes now realised in many labs.
assessment.attribution: A clean two-person theory pair with decisive contributions; experimental realisation by Wineland's and Blatt's groups is a partner contribution (Wineland was already awarded in 2012). Overlap with B010, B023 and B039 in credit lists means the same names appear in several candidates.
assessment.maturity: Experimentally realised and mature; recognition could be considered overdue. Quantum simulation successes are real, though quantum advantage in useful tasks is still unsettled.
uncertainties: Theory-only prize may be seen as less compelling than experiment; I generally prefer discoveries from nature.
Overlap with other candidates and with experimentalists (Blatt, Monroe).

assessment.nobel_worthiness: IceCube opened neutrino astronomy by detecting high-energy astrophysical neutrinos, with later evidence of a blazar (TXS 0506+056) and the Galactic plane. A genuine discovery from nature that opened a new window; it follows the 2002 prize for cosmic neutrinos.
assessment.attribution: Halzen is the project's scientific leader; Karle and Spiering were central in the collaboration and the predecessor AMANDA. A three-person configuration is plausible but collaboration contributions make attribution uncertain.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed by independent analyses and a growing set of source associations, but sources of most of the flux are still unidentified. Probably somewhat premature in terms of astrophysical interpretation, yet the discovery itself is solid.
uncertainties: Identification of the sources is incomplete.
Large-collaboration credit; the role of Spiering versus other IceCube leaders is something I cannot verify.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Spectroscopic detection of exoplanet atmospheres (sodium, then molecules by transmission and emission spectroscopy) turned exoplanets into physical objects, and bears on the question of life elsewhere. The existential dimension is high, and it builds on the 2019 exoplanet recognition.
assessment.attribution: Seager's early theoretical predictions, Charbonneau's first detection, and Deming's emission work form a reasonable trio; Brown and others contributed. Credit is somewhat distributed.
assessment.maturity: Strengthened by JWST results, but the field is rapidly changing and the claims for biosignatures are not mature. The 2019 prize reduces room.
uncertainties: Whether the field has a single decisive discovery.
Disputed claims in individual atmospheric detections.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Pulsar timing arrays found evidence for a nanohertz gravitational-wave background, a new window on gravitation at an entirely different frequency from LIGO, probably from supermassive binaries. It is a gravity result obtained from nature, as I like.
assessment.attribution: Evidence was reported in 2023 by NANOGrav, EPTA/InPTA, PPTA and CPTA; the supplied names correspond to the leaders of different arrays, which makes any three-person choice contestable. Hellings-Downs correlation work and earlier pulsar timing pioneers also matter.
assessment.maturity: Evidence is roughly 2 to 4 sigma per array; no individual source is detected, and origin (supermassive binaries versus new physics) is not settled. Likely premature for a prize.
uncertainties: Significance below the conventional discovery standard.
Astrophysical versus cosmological origin of the signal.
